The Period of the Rise of Islam
Or were they established by reason itself, in the sense that the religious texts had already stated those beliefs together with their rational proofs?
The Period of the Rise of Islam

We mention this observation because it strongly shows that even when rational inquiry flourished in the hands of the theologians, the theologians themselves remained tied to the earlier view of knowledge.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
As the observation above shows, they still accepted one of two positions.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
Either religious beliefs were established by revealed law and reason understood them through that revelation.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
Or they were “established by reason,” but only in the sense that the religious texts had already laid down the rational arguments for them.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
Even the second position therefore assumes that the rational proofs themselves were already given in advance by religious texts.
The Period of the Rise of Islam

If we look for the social and ideological basis of this position in its two forms, we find it in the need to preserve and strengthen the ideology of the new social group whose position in the developing social and class structure was supported by the idea that knowledge rested on faith.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
The Period of the Rise of Islam
We should avoid making an absolute claim here. An absolute way of thinking is foreign to scientific method.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
We therefore need to distinguish between two different attitudes in Islam and among Muslims toward knowledge.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
One concerned matters of religious belief.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
The other concerned matters of law and legislation, where rational inquiry was used to some extent.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
There was, in fact, a difference between the two.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
Questions of religious belief were centered on receiving knowledge from divine revelation without debate and without independent rational inquiry.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
But in matters of law, we find some use of ijtihād—reasoned judgment—which in some respects is a form of rational thought.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
How did Muslims distinguish between these two areas?
The Period of the Rise of Islam
The distinction arose from a belief held among Muslims from the earliest period.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
Everything concerning the basic principles of faith was believed to have been completely revealed by God, leaving nothing for independent reason to decide.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
The position of Islamic law was different.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
Its basic principles had also been completed through revelation, but reason still had a role in working out the details of those principles and applying them to particular cases.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
This use of reason is what Muslims call ijtihād.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
It means using the mind to apply general principles to new and particular situations that continually arise in the constantly changing course of everyday life.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
Ibn ʿAbd al-Barr explains the difference between the two areas as follows:
The Period of the Rise of Islam

“The early Muslims—may God have mercy on them—forbade disputation about God ... and His attributes. But as for jurisprudence, meaning the science of religious law, they agreed that debate and discussion were permissible in it, because it requires particular cases to be referred back to general principles whenever necessary. Matters of belief are not like this, because according to the community—that is, the people of the Sunna—God ... may only be described as He described Himself, or as His Messenger described Him ... and as the community agreed.”
The Period of the Rise of Islam
Once belief and religious law are distinguished in this way, a space opens for reason to operate within one part of Islam.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
Reasoning through ijtihād in matters of law is not simply a mechanical process of applying general rules to particular cases.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
The Period of the Rise of Islam
It requires finding similarities and relevant parallels between cases when reasoning by analogy, or qiyās.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
It also requires identifying the reasons behind legal rulings found in the texts and from which general principles were formed.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
Then, when a new case appears, one must investigate whether the same reason exists in that case. Only then can one decide whether the general rule should or should not be applied.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
Ijtihād carried out under these conditions is therefore a genuine form of thinking.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
But this form of thought remains strictly controlled by rules laid down for it from outside the process of reasoning itself.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
It does not work according to rules that reason discovers independently, through its own powers of knowledge, by studying the objective movement of the world.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
4 — A Seed of a “Theory of Knowledge” in the Qurʾān?
The Period of the Rise of Islam
There is another side to the question of knowledge in Islam that may lead us to reconsider some of our earlier conclusions.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
It may even allow us to accept Ibn Ḥazm’s statement that knowledge is acquired rather than simply given.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
A modern Arab researcher has drawn attention to this side of the question.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
He points to two Qurʾānic verses:
The Period of the Rise of Islam
“God brought you out of your mothers’ wombs knowing nothing, and gave you hearing, sight, and hearts, so that you might give thanks.” (Qurʾān 16:78)
The Period of the Rise of Islam
“Have they not traveled through the land, so that they might have hearts with which to understand, or ears with which to hear...?” (Qurʾān 22:46)
The Period of the Rise of Islam
The researcher says that these verses, and others like them,
The Period of the Rise of Islam
“show that human beings possess faculties through which they understand things, including hearing, sight, and the heart—that is, reason.”
The Period of the Rise of Islam
Human knowledge therefore depends on these faculties.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
In this sense, knowledge is acquired.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
The Qurʾān would therefore contain the seed of a theory of knowledge that we will later see developed in detail by the philosophers.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
It is true that the Qurʾān clearly gives an important role to the direct senses in gaining sensory knowledge.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
It is also true that these verses appear to present such knowledge as acquired, in the sense intended by Ibn Ḥazm.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
That is, people gain it through experience by using their natural powers of perception in the fields appropriate to each one.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
But the context in which these verses appear determines their meaning and purpose.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
That Qurʾānic context shows that sensory knowledge gained through these powers of perception is meant to provide the mind with evidence from the visible world and its great observable phenomena.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
This evidence is then used to support religious faith and confirm the beliefs taught by Islam as truths received through divine revelation.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
Even so, this does not prevent us from making another point.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
The Qurʾān’s concern with using reason to support religious belief, drawing on knowledge gained through the senses, can itself be counted in reason’s favor.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
At the very least, it recognizes the need to support faith through reason.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
But the question now is this: does that observation undermine the claim that the Qur’an contains the beginnings of a theory of knowledge?
The Period of the Rise of Islam

It does not seem to. The social meaning of the verses we discussed still gives knowledge gained through the senses a genuine role in the process of knowing. Sensory perception forms one stage in the chain of thought. It carries the mind forward to another stage until it reaches the conclusion being sought—which, in this case, is support for faith.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
5 — The Question of the “Glorification of Reason” in the Qur’an
The Period of the Rise of Islam

There is another question about Islam’s attitude toward knowledge that we need to examine if we want to cover the subject fully. This is the Qur’anic phenomenon often described as the “glorification of reason.” Alongside it is what one contemporary Arab researcher calls “the Prophet’s endorsement of reason in many hadiths.” This is a striking question, and it deserves attention.
The Period of the Rise of Islam

The Qur’an contains many verses that praise the use of reason. People are called on to think about the universe and to reflect on the great mysteries found in the heavens and the earth. Other verses condemn those who have hearts—meaning minds—“with which they do not understand.” They are compared to cattle and described as “even further astray.”
The Period of the Rise of Islam
So the Qur’an did not ignore reason or deny its role as a tool of thought. The many verses of this kind show quite the opposite.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
But how far does the Qur’an allow reason to go in seeking knowledge on its own?
The Period of the Rise of Islam

Knowledge in Islam is confined within certain limits that reason is not allowed to cross. This means that the Qur’an’s “glorification of reason,” and the Prophet’s praise of reason in the hadiths, also has a limited scope.
The Period of the Rise of Islam

This gives us reason to question the claim that rational thought could never be erased from Arab-Islamic civilization for one reason alone: because it came from the earliest sources of Islam, above all the Qur’an. According to this view:
The Period of the Rise of Islam

If rational thought had been merely a passing development, or simply one result of the interactions Arab civilization experienced through contact with other civilizations, this value could have been erased or pushed aside. But because it was organically tied to the first and sacred source of Islamic thought—the Qur’an—and because the Prophet also endorsed reason in many hadiths, rational thought, and therefore philosophical thought, became an authentic value in intellectual life. It might retreat for a time, fall behind for a period, or go through moments of decline, but it could never be uprooted or made to disappear.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
This argument can be questioned from several directions.
The Period of the Rise of Islam

First, and most importantly, it separates two elements that both helped form “rational thought in Arab-Islamic civilization”: the original source of Islamic thought, on the one hand, and “the effects of the interactions that Arab civilization acquired through contact with other civilizations,” on the other.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
A sound method requires us to see both of these as organic and formative parts of Arab-Islamic civilization itself.
The Period of the Rise of Islam

Second, the argument seems to treat the influence of other civilizations as something accidental or secondary within Arab-Islamic rational thought. But, as we have said, that influence was itself an organic part of the formation and unity of this thought. It is therefore unrealistic to say that the earliest Islamic sources were the only reason rational thought could never be erased from this civilization.
The Period of the Rise of Islam

Third, we certainly need to recognize the deep influence that the earliest Islamic sources had on the formation of this rational tradition. But if we want to understand why this “authentic value in intellectual life” could not simply be uprooted and destroyed, we need to look for the real reason in the movement of society itself: in the development of Arab society and in Islam’s objective relationship to that development.
The Period of the Rise of Islam

Finally, the earliest sources of Islam themselves did not allow reason to go beyond certain limits in its independent search for knowledge. Those limits were set by the relationship Islam established between knowledge and faith.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
6 — Knowledge in the Course of Development
The Period of the Rise of Islam

After everything we have concluded and discussed about knowledge in Islam, and especially about the relationship between faith and knowledge—the relationship that tied knowledge completely to religious belief—we now need to ask:
The Period of the Rise of Islam
Do these conclusions mean that the development of Arab thought was interrupted, or even brought to a halt, during the first period of Islam?
The Period of the Rise of Islam
The way this question is phrased assumes that Arab thought had already been developing before Islam and that its development had been moving forward with history.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
The Period of the Rise of Islam

In fact, Arab thought was moving through a process of historical development during the period immediately before the rise of Islam, as we explained in detail earlier. This development included its religious and metaphysical ideas.
The Period of the Rise of Islam

No old or modern Muslim thinker has denied this fact. We have already seen writers such as al-Shahrastānī, Qāḍī Ṣāʿid, Ibn Khaldūn and Muṣṭafā ʿAbd al-Rāziq discuss different features of pre-Islamic culture and the kind of thinking found within it. Some of the examples they mention concern the metaphysics of existence.
The Period of the Rise of Islam

One statement by ʿAbd al-Rāziq is especially worth noting. He says that, when the Qur’an was revealed, the Arabs “were engaged in disputes and debates over beliefs, and questions concerning the sending of prophets, life, the afterlife, and the resurrection of bodies after death were particularly debated among the different religious groups.”
The Period of the Rise of Islam
So Arab thought in the pre-Islamic period was moving along the path of development that we described in the first chapter.
The Period of the Rise of Islam

At that stage, however, knowledge had not yet been tied by the pre-Islamic “thinker” or “sage” to one fixed and final source in the way it was during the first period of Islam. In other words, the particular relationship between faith and knowledge that we have been discussing had not yet appeared.
The Period of the Rise of Islam

That is why the question we asked above is a legitimate one. Once knowledge became tied to faith in this new way, it is understandable that someone might imagine that some kind of break or pause had taken place in the development of Arab thought.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
So how should we understand the problem?
The Period of the Rise of Islam

The mistake in this view is that it looks at the Islamic relationship between knowledge and faith from only one side. It takes that relationship in isolation, instead of looking at the other forces affecting knowledge during the first period of Islam, or at the broader set of developments that together formed the new course of Arab-Islamic thought.
The Period of the Rise of Islam

The connection between knowledge and faith—whether we call it faith-based knowledge, knowledge-based faith, or simply the combination of the two—was not, first of all, completely disconnected from the historical form that knowledge had already taken during the pre-Islamic period.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
By this I mean that connecting knowledge to a world beyond nature was not something entirely foreign to late pre-Islamic thought, especially after the spread of the Hanif movement.
The Period of the Rise of Islam

Second, Islam appeared under the historical conditions we examined in the previous chapter. Those conditions placed this inherited form of knowledge within a changing social reality. That social reality was drawing together a whole range of developments that historical conditions were bringing into being and combining them within one overall process of change.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
If we look at knowledge within this broader movement, its connection with faith no longer appears as a break in the development of Arab thought.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
This connection did not develop separately from the wider movement of history. It was itself one of the forms produced by the historical conditions we have described.
The Period of the Rise of Islam

From this point of view, we also need to notice that Arab thought in the early Islamic period was beginning to move beyond the simplicity and strongly sense-based character that had generally marked it before. It was entering a more complex and structured stage.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
At this new stage, the process of knowing began, relatively speaking, to move from a framework dominated by sensory images toward one that gave a larger role to mental abstraction.
